extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors; young men considering literature as a vocation; literary practitioners and would-be professional writers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and prescriptive standards for men who contemplate literature as a profession: how to preserve integrity, when to publish, how to relate to publishers and the market, and what counts as worthwhile literary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve mental and physical independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspiring writers should "preserve, as above all price, your proper independence, mental and physical."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn a good trade or handicraft first so you can fall back on it; make yourself self-subsisting and skilful with the hands so you need not sell your integrity for bread. Specific advice: take work in field or shop, master duties, secure a patch of ground or other manual occupation to support yourself while improving your mental powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not degrade your faculty into beggary
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid becoming the 'literary mendicant' who wanders publisher to publisher or begs readers for payment for unsolicited poems or essays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: petitioning editors for printing, hawking one's work, or expecting payment for unsolicited pieces. Author should refuse to 'degrade my faculty of uttering thoughts ... into a means of indirect beggary' and should not solicit exchange of others' bread for his thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: A new book must communicate a new truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "A new book is only to be justified by a new truth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before publishing, be able to answer: 'What proposition is this book intended to set forth and commend? What fact does it reveal? What is its drift, its purport?' Examples of valid new contributions include firsthand routes or practical technical knowledge (e.g., travel route, charcoal-making methods). If a book adds nothing to facts or ideas, it is harmful and should not be produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the peril of compliance (writing for today's market)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ever-present and fearful peril of the Literary vocation is compliance! the sacrifice of the eternal verity to the temporary necessity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing to earn immediate bread forces you to produce what the market currently appreciates, tending toward moral indifference and debasement. Selling one's mental faculties to the highest cash bidder makes it unlikely one will be doing 'Divine work'; resist going to market whenever it would force you to compromise truth or long-term integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse continual use with improvement of faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent production or continual use of literary faculties does not necessarily create or improve genuine literary qualities; use can exhaust as often as strengthen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitative, mechanical drudgery as a journeyman writer will not create truly great qualities. If great qualities inhere, they will find their way out; if not, they cannot be manufactured by mere practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing is an intellectual vocation requiring skill and capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing itself is a pursuit requiring 'various talents, ripe scholarship, large capital, and rare sagacity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should recognize that bringing out and selling a book often demands as much ability as writing it. Many original publications lose money; success in publishing is as rare as in authorship. This justifies publishers' caution and the economic realities of the trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-scrutiny before blaming publishers/audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who complain of publishers' obtuseness or readers' indifference should first judge whether their own work merits attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: blaming publishers for not discovering merit while not having read or supported other authors. Many complaints come from those whose work is unreadable; authors should ask whether their writing is genuinely good before blaming external factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept patient fortune if your genius must create its audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors (e.g., Wordsworth) write for a public their genius must create or patience must await; they accept their fortune calmly without seeking immediate popularity or pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a legitimate stance: do your work steadfastly and without repining if immediate reward is absent. Do not pursue simultaneous service to both 'God and Mammon'; accept delayed recognition if the work is profound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical, humble contributions are legitimate literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Any contribution to knowledge of nature or to practical methods (however rude or humble) is beneficent and worthy of regard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a shipwreck survivor describing a new overland route; a charcoal-maker explaining burning techniques. Such concrete, novel information can justify publication even if the author is otherwise 'illiterate and commonplace.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing merely to be readable/salable is morally suspect
rubrics_metrics.description: If a book's only aim is to be readable and thus salable (to 'win gold for its author and his accomplices'), it is not justified and should be suppressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay suggests extreme remedy (burn the manuscript) for works produced solely for sale. Authors must ensure high aims and genuine contributions rather than producing literature as a commodity alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain self-respect; avoid humiliating appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: True genius produces a healthful pride that would revolt against hawking one’s 'Diviner faculties'; lacking that, appeals to pity or scandalous self-exposure indicate lack of self-respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include public complaints about 'Calamities of Genius', begging for patronage without dignity, or converting authorship into an escape from manual labor. Self-respect should govern how one seeks livelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: International copyright and fair payment for foreign works
rubrics_metrics.description: The denial of international copyright is unjust: it allows national appropriation of foreign authors' works without equivalent payment and harms domestic authors by cheap competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy criterion: respecting international copyright is morally right and economically important to sustain domestic authors' compensation and formation of national mind. The essay argues this is a national injury and an issue of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great authors must keep moral responsibility; vices are especially damaging
rubrics_metrics.description: The frailties and vices of great authors (drunkenness, libertinism, corruption) are lamentable because their public lives make such faults more visible and enduring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those gifted and prominent should avoid misconduct because their errors overshadow their achievements and invite public scorn; moral integrity is part of the vocation's duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors provide an enduring cultural power; strive for noble, lasting work
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing nobly and excellently is a loftier achievement than ruling or conquest; great books endure across generations and shape mind and morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for work that will instruct and delight future ages (examples: Book of Job, Cicero, Virgil, Plato). This is an aspirational standard: pursue enduring excellence rather than ephemeral success.
